I have two girls ready to harvest in two weeks but I have to be away for work. I don't want to leave the lights on while I'm away for fear of fire. Does it hurt them to be in the dark that long? I know that it's common to leave them in the dark for 48h before harvest. But 96h?

[Update]: They took it well and I had a great harvest today, I will post a report on my second grow later.
Will it hurt my girls if I leave them in the dark for 4 days?

Yes it will hurt them. The effect it will have on them will depend on the individual plants and the other conditions available but typically they'll stretch out like mad, the stems will weaken a little from the stretch, the leaves will point up like they're trying to claw their way out of the ground after being buried and the plant will become super sensitive to light making the chances of burning/bleaching it very likely once the light is turned back on. It can totally be done and you can minimize the potential harm considerably but if you can avoid turning the light off it would be recommended that you don't turn it off. The chances of a fire are slim to none if you have set everything up properly, ie. all electrical equipment elevated and away from all water sources, good amounts of air flow, etc. You also have to keep in mind that a small fire will produce considerably more smoke than you would imagine and that someone will likely call the fire department even if you manage to get it put out pretty quickly. They've seen grow room fires before and tend to report them to LEO so personally I'd rather let the fire sanitize the area by letting the place burn to the ground than I would trying to save the garden and hiding everything before arrive because there is no way you're going to beat them when they're legally allowed to ignore road rules to get to the scene ASAP. So with the best option being let the place burn I'd just put my faith in my setup to not self combust and put the light on a timer.

absolutely this. lots of stretching and the unseen beast that scares us all. Stress. You don't want to stress it so bad (with whatever variables) that it goes herm on you. Stress has also been known to underproduce on yields at harvest. Good luck!

They won't have time to herm on me. After those 4 days they are ripe for harvest anyway and since it's considered beneficial for them to be left in the dark for 48h prior to harvest. I thought 2 more days wouldn't hurt.

First, I have nothing against the rights of any individuals, and I do not have anything against people being able to love/marry/whatever whomever they choose. BUT...

The Court has decided a major issue with more massive implications than people seem to grasp on its face. This is larger than simply granting "equality," or whatever the proper term is, to certain individuals. The Court has directly affronted Federalism.

With this opinion, the Court has essentially taken the power of the states to regulate internally. Marriage, considered part of family law, has been an issue decided by, at least traditionally, state jurisdiction. This, along with the Police Power, had always been under state control.

However, the Federal Government has long been taking power from the states (e.g. post-Lochner Era) and cutting the rights the states have. The obvious infringement on state rights is the abuse of the commerce clause to allow congress to control anything even remotely touching interstate commerce. (E.g., inter alia, Gonzales v. Raich)

The problem with the SCotUS forcing every state to not only allow but marry couples of the same biology is that it infringes on the state's right to decide on how it acts. By disallowing the states to decide what is and is not acceptable within their borders, the federal government is assuming power it did not have. It is a slippery-slope that states continue to lose their rights to control their own interests one at a time. What now stops the federal government from deciding what is relegated to state issues? Nothing, since every issue can potentially been made into a constitutional one, and the federal government merely has to give deference to state government when it feels like it.

Also, there is another slippery-slope argument to be made: now that the government allows this type of marriage, how can it deny any further types? Why not recognize a three person marriage? Or more? Will polygamy be legalized? One cannot say that it is based on societal norms because those are gone: states are not allowed to dictate what is "equality", so how can the Constitution discriminate against such "basic human rights"? It can't. Allowing such marriages (or further) is the next logical step.

The federal government has now given itself a license to write the law for itself and the states. Before, the people [indirectly] created the law of their jurisdiction, and if they didn't like it, they could change it or leave. Now, the federal government simply tells states what the law is. The system of federal balancing state and vice versa is now one-sided, with the federal in complete control. Is this the type of government the country is supposed to have. I don't believe so.

I support individual rights to the fullest extent, and I harbor no ill will towards anyone by their lifestyle, but I also support the legal system the country was meant to have.

To anyone interested in the subject of constitutional interpretation and the history of the Supreme Court, I recommend taking a constitutional law course.

Lastly, please feel free to tell me if I am wrong on any of these legal matters.
